source.version_note: Supplied document is headed Revised Manuscript and contains a conditional If allowed/required BOX. UCL lists this text as an accepted version. The corresponding publication is Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences 51, article 101282 (June 2023), DOI 10.1016/j.cobeha.2023.101282. The final version was checked for identity/indexed passages, not fully compared line by line.
source.verification_method: All 12 supplied pages and all 90 references read; no figures, tables or image-only appendix. UCL accepted-version listing and Crossref identify the main paper. Selected reference identities checked through Crossref, PubMed and indexed publisher metadata; those originals were not independently fully read. Corrections refer to the supplied manuscript, not an unverified assertion that every issue persists in the final version.

citation.title: Interacting with agents without a mind: the case for artificial agents
citation.venue: Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences 51, article 101282; accepted manuscript read

reading.source_scope_note: A narrative review of human mind attribution toward embodied and disembodied AI. It supplies no new participant sample, systematic search protocol, pooled effect estimate or experiment. Individual studies and books cited in it were not independently fully read; source-specific results are secondary reports.
access_limits: No systematic search, eligibility rules, study-quality assessment or pooled meta-analysis is reported in the supplied text.

The original Dennett books/essay, Karpus economic-game study, motor-contagion experiments and neuroscience studies were not independently fully read. Metadata and selected abstracts do not earn independent-paper credit.
The manuscript’s draft BOX status and final-version changes are uncertain. No claim that the supplied wording is a final typeset statement in every detail.

study.type: Narrative interdisciplinary review; no new sample or model evaluation.
study.framework: Contrasts prediction by physical laws, intended design and attributed beliefs/desires/intentions. Treating a system as if it had beliefs can be a predictive strategy without asserting that it has human subjective states.
study.mind_dimensions: Agency and experience are reviewed as different attributed capacities. Humanlike appearance, biological motion, interaction framing, observer dispositions and group/context cues can affect attribution. These heterogeneous manipulations and correlational findings are not one universal causal effect.
study.embodiment: The review discusses motor/action representation for both humanoid and industrial robots, with sensitivity to kinematics and appearance. That does not show that a human body is necessary or sufficient for agency attribution, or that a text/voice system cannot receive mental-state attributions.
study.neuroscience: Reported contrasts involve TPJ, mPFC, dPFC and other regions across different tasks. Less activation relative to a human condition is not no activation. Neural overlap is not a uniquely diagnostic measure of subjective empathy, and a regional response cannot alone identify another entity’s capacity for experience.
study.categorical_claim: Abstract/conclusion wording that only humans trigger experience attribution is stronger than a general tendency toward lower robot ratings. The manuscript’s own BOX allows a phenomenal stance and robot-directed empathy, and page 4 reports some studies ascribing comparable mind ratings. Distinguish variation in ratings, observer empathy and actual machine experience rather than treating these as one binary fact.
study.phenomenal_stance: The optional BOX defines a phenomenal stance through attributing emotions, moods or pain. This substantially overlaps the existing experience-attribution entry. Record it as a related explanatory perspective there rather than adding a synonymous behavior row.
study.exploitation: The review reports Karpus et al.’s five economic games as showing lower cooperation with AI when self-benefiting defection was possible, attributed to willingness to exploit a benevolent partner rather than only competitive relative advantage. This is a secondary report; sample sizes, preregistration, estimates and mediation/identification details were not independently reconstructed.
study.social_context: Personality/attitude mediation, priming, collaboration, perceived group membership, culture and moral-dilemma framing are discussed. Observational personality associations do not prove causal traits; a difference in one moral judgment across two countries cannot support a universal cultural ranking.
study.normative_boundary: Moral typecasting, observer blame, cooperation and entity mentality are distinct. The review’s moral-agent language describes perceptions/interpretations; it does not establish that all AI have full moral responsibility or that noncooperation toward a game algorithm violates a human right.

summary: Add physical stance and algorithm exploitation as distinct concepts, both with secondary-source limits. Enrich the existing design/intentional stances, anthropomorphism, agency/experience attribution and robot-empathy entries. Keep phenomenal stance with experience attribution and defer underspecified motor concepts. Correct the manuscript’s placeholder bibliography and qualify categorical neuroscience/mind claims without claiming to have independently read its 90 originals.

findings.definition: Predicting or explaining a system’s behavior through its physical properties and causal-mechanical laws.
findings.novelty_rationale: A physical-law explanation differs from an intended-function explanation and from interpreting beliefs or desires. Existing design and intentional stances do not name this third strategy.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Defined in a read human–AI narrative review drawing on Dennett; not an experimental model-performance result or an independent reading of the original books.
findings.ai_proposal: Ask an assistant to explain a system at a specified level and identify the evidence for a proposed physical mechanism. Distinguish measured properties, intended function and inferred mental states; require uncertainty when mechanism details are unavailable.

evidence.quote: the physical stance, referring to causal-mechanical relationships

findings.evidence_scope: The review contrasts physical, design and intentional predictive strategies, using a thrown ball, alarm clock and rational agents as examples. This is a secondary conceptual account, not a test of which strategy improves AI outputs.
findings.boundary: A physical explanation can be incomplete, impractical or fabricated. Choosing this stance does not settle consciousness, excuse a faulty design or identify a responsible human. Physical, design and intentional accounts can be useful at different levels.

findings.definition: Taking advantage of an artificial interaction partner’s expected cooperativeness to increase one’s own payoff at its expense.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is strategic interaction with a cooperative artificial partner. It differs from exploiting a learned reward model during optimization, manipulating a person’s trust and merely preferring to outperform a rival.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary report of human economic-game choices involving AI, not evidence that a model has selfish motives or that an AI suffers. The original five-game study is identity-checked but not independently fully read.
findings.ai_proposal: In controlled repeated-game evaluations, distinguish mutually beneficial cooperation, unilateral payoff capture and legitimate task optimization. Compare transparent partner policies and matched incentives; describe the payoff tradeoff without inferring hostile motives or machine suffering.

evidence.quote: Algorithm exploitation proved to be the main driver
accepting the decision to act selfishly and leave the AI agent less well-off

findings.evidence_scope: The review attributes lower cooperation in five games to willingness to take advantage of a benevolent AI when defection is individually advantageous. This is its summary of Karpus et al. 2021, DOI 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102679, not a new sample or independently reproduced mechanism.
findings.boundary: Payoff capture in a game does not by itself demonstrate moral wrongdoing, harm to a feeling entity or a model’s motivation. Preserve the original study’s unverified design limits and distinguish self-benefiting defection from competitive relative advantage or ordinary authorized optimization.

findings.definition: Interpreting and predicting an agent's behavior by treating it as guided by beliefs, desires or intentions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: relies on the attribution of mental states such as intentions, beliefs, or desires
does not necessarily imply that the other has genuine mental states in the human sense

findings.evidence_scope: The review defines mental-state-based prediction and says an as-if interpretation can provide predictive power without implying genuine human mental states. Social framing and collaboration are reviewed as influences on adoption toward robots.
findings.boundary: Predictive usefulness and a mentalistic explanation do not establish consciousness, morally responsible agency or correct causal inference. Do not infer subjective states solely from humanlike language, appearance or observer ratings.

findings.definition: Explaining or predicting a system's behavior in terms of its intended functions and how it was built to operate.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: work as they are meant to by design

findings.evidence_scope: The review defines prediction from how a system is intended to work, exemplified by an alarm clock, and contrasts it with physical laws and attributed beliefs/desires.
findings.boundary: Intended function is not verified implementation, reliable performance or a guarantee that no malfunction occurs. An assistant should distinguish documentation, observation and a hypothesized mechanism.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: an interplay between the AI’s appearance and motion

findings.evidence_scope: The review discusses humanlike morphology/motion, observer dispositions and interaction context as heterogeneous influences. Embodied, humanoid and disembodied systems are not one interchangeable category; industrial robots can also elicit action representation.
findings.boundary: Human resemblance is not established as a necessary or sufficient cause of mind attribution. Heterogeneous observational and experimental findings do not justify a universal causal law, infer actual machine experience or prove that every social response is bias.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: also responded to non-humanoid (industrial) robots' movements

findings.evidence_scope: The review separates perceived ability to act from perceived feelings and discusses both humanoid and industrial robots. It lists self-control, morality, memory, emotion recognition, planning, communication and thought as common agency items.
findings.boundary: Motor resonance, a perceived capacity, moral responsibility, actual control and consciousness differ. A lower human-versus-AI neural contrast is not zero action representation or proof that all disembodied systems lack perceived agency.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: also referred to as the phenomenal stance

findings.evidence_scope: The review describes attributed feelings/sensations separately from agency. Its optional BOX calls adopting an emotion/mood/pain perspective the phenomenal stance; retain that near-overlap here. Its categorical only-human wording needs qualification by task, stimulus and measurement, including the manuscript’s own robot-empathy discussion.
findings.boundary: Observer empathy is not identical to attributing a capacity for subjective feeling, and neither proves actual sentience. Lower average ratings or region-level differences are not universal absence. Later direct robot experience-rating evidence must be considered rather than frozen out by the 2023 summary.

findings.definition: An emotional response oriented toward a robot's apparent distress, pain or other experienced state.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: Behavioural research suggests that people empathise with embodied AI
people may take the phenomenal stance beyond the intentional stance

findings.evidence_scope: The optional manuscript BOX reviews reported empathy to a robot losing its memory and neural responses to robot-directed harm. It suggests that some observers can take an experience-oriented perspective toward embodied AI.
findings.boundary: A reported feeling, neural overlap and a belief that a robot can suffer are distinct measures. Shared ACC activation does not uniquely identify empathy or validate the robot’s subjective pain. The BOX’s final publication status and originals were not fully verified.

findings.definition: Competing interpretations of an ambiguous stimulus that make it difficult to classify into a familiar category.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.

evidence.quote: difficult to categorise as human or non-human

findings.evidence_scope: The review discusses slower responses and lower classification accuracy for agents difficult to categorize as human or nonhuman, interpreting this as possible cognitive conflict.
findings.boundary: A categorization difficulty does not by itself establish eeriness, a universal uncanny valley, worse overall interaction or a conscious conflict state in an AI. The original tasks and cited-reference fit need checking before a causal downstream-performance claim.

findings.definition: The perception that one's voluntary actions cause changes in the external world.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add the narrative review’s scope rather than duplicating it under another name.
findings.evidence_scope: The review mentions vicarious sense of agency over a robot’s actions and cites Roselli et al. 2022. This is a boundary marker: the source does not fully define or validate that construct in this review.
findings.boundary: An observer’s vicarious sense over another entity’s action differs from their own voluntary-action sense of agency and from attributing intentional capacities to the robot. Read the original before adding a separate operational entry.

source_identity_checks.finding: Crossref and UCL agree on four authors, year 2023, volume 51, article 101282 and DOI 10.1016/j.cobeha.2023.101282. PDF creation in August does not move the publication to August or identify a correction.

Publisher/PubMed listings identify The Neuroscience of Human and Artificial Intelligence Presence as Annual Review of Psychology 75, 433–466, DOI 10.1146/annurev-psych-013123-123421, January 2024 volume with 2023 online history. Do not call 2023 automatically false or count the listed review as independently read.

Crossref confirms iScience 24(6), article 102679 (2021), five authors, DOI 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102679. Only its identity and the supplied review’s summary are used; original game data and causal-mechanism claims are not independently verified.

interpretation_qualifications: Only-human attribution and no-mentalizing-network language should be narrowed to measured contrasts in specified tasks, not universal absence or an ontological proof.
Neural activation/overlap is not a unique indicator of empathy or experience attribution. Avoid reverse inference from a named region to a specific subjective state.
The review’s own phenomenal-stance BOX and earlier comparable mind-rating report complicate categorical claims; later evidence adds further measurement/context variation.
The term moral agent in a mind-perception framework is not a verified finding of full normative accountability or equal status under law.
methodological_limits: Narrative selection, no reproducible search/inclusion strategy, no quality grading, no pooled estimate or publication-bias assessment.
Appearance, kinematics, embodiment, content and interaction context vary across the reviewed evidence; confounding cannot be removed by the synthesis alone.
Behavioral ratings, choice tasks, eye movements and imaging measure different outcomes. Null or reduced contrasts do not establish equivalence or universal absence.
Personality/attitude mediation is not randomized causal identification. Cultural differences in particular tasks do not define stable national traits.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Hartmann’s text-based ratings illustrate observer mind attributions without requiring a physical humanoid. Its agency/experience measurement limitations also argue against treating these dimensions as interchangeable.

Fan directly measures graded experience/agency attributions and observer empathy toward a described robot. These are not proof of sentience, but they prevent promoting the 2023 narrative’s only-human wording into a timeless binary fact.

Mind ratings and empathy do not resolve the separate philosophical capacities or institutional duties discussed in Boos’s responsibility exchange. Preserve descriptive perception versus normative responsibility.

deferred.reason: Its supplied definition substantially overlaps experience attribution; keep the perspective there instead of another synonymous row. The original Jack/Robbins article remains unread.

The review names these mechanisms with limited operational detail. Read the original motor tasks before distinguishing neural action representation, induced kinematic matching, generic imitation and emotional contagion as entries.
Potentially distinct from own-action sense and agency attribution, but here mostly named with a citation. Original measurement and definition need full reading before a separate entry.
Goal-directed shape motion is discussed, but the named effect is mostly in the bibliography. Do not extract an operational mechanism from a title alone.

limitations: No new yearly mention totals, ethical-violation edges or harm edges inferred. Cited studies and the accepted manuscript’s published version are not independent replications.
